A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DASB, retaining its core benchmark design and overlapping speech experiments. The text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion.

before.justification: v1 reports original downstream speech experiments and audio reconstruction evaluations in Tables 2-4 and Appendices D-E.

after.justification: v3 reports original speech, music and general-audio evaluations, embedding-initialization experiments and TTS sampling analyses in Tables 2-4 and 9-12 and Appendix H.

M1.justification: The frozen encoder, attention-based combination, downstream model and decoder framework remains. v3 adds a localized SQ-Codec adaptation using ternary-matrix dequantization and concatenated group embeddings, and introduces a VALL-E-based TTS path with residual prediction. These extend the retained framework rather than replace its central procedure.

E1.justification: v3 retains the speech suite and adds ESC-50 and UrbanSound8K sound classification, GTZAN genre and music-versus-speech classification, NSynth pitch classification, MUSDB music separation, FUSS general-sound separation and LibriTTS multi-speaker TTS. These substantially expand the represented domains and task requirements beyond v1's speech-only evaluations.

E2.justification: v3 retains the six original tokenizers and adds Mimi, SQ-Codec and WavTokenizer to the speech comparisons. New-domain evaluations introduce BEATs, MERT, DEMUCS and TDCN++ baselines. Generative tables also add unprocessed-mixture controls, while the reconstruction comparison replaces v1's continuous-SSL reference with ground-truth audio.

E3.justification: The reported English-ASR training split changes from train-clean-100 to 'train-clean-960'; Branchformer replaces ContextNet and the low-resource linear head, and character-only outputs gain BPE alternatives. Multi-speaker TTS introduces phoneme inputs and a different architecture and dataset. Reconstruction evaluation changes from DNSMOS/dWER to UTMOS/WER, and Appendix H adds a 100-sample inference-parameter search.

E4.justification: v1 already analyzes bitrate, downstream architectures and reconstruction. v3 adds random-versus-encoder-based embedding initialization experiments for ASR and keyword spotting (Table 12), TTS top-k and temperature sensitivity experiments (Figures 4-5), and revised reconstruction diagnostics (Appendix F). These substantially expand the questions investigated beyond the original analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without run counts or uncertainty estimates. v3 states that evaluations use three random seeds and presents averaged results with widespread ± values, alongside discussion of training variability. This is newly documented repeated-run evidence, not an established increase from a known v1 run count; the meaning of ± is not explicitly defined.

E6.justification: Many speech scores are replaced, and extensive new-domain, tokenizer, initialization and sampling results are added. For six-codebook Discrete WavLM with the BiLSTM ASR head, test-clean WER changes from 8.52 in v1 Table 9 to 4.32 ± 0.23 in v3 Table 2. The changed training split and protocol prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: The bitrate definition and attention equations are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3's additional mechanism explanations and ranking descriptions do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning or formal guarantees.

C1.justification: v3 broadens the central contribution from a speech benchmark to evaluation across speech, music and general audio. It adds prominent claims that direct token evaluation isolates quantization loss and that discrete representations require careful scaling and tuning because of weaker robustness. The general semantic-token advantage and gap relative to continuous representations remain central.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands explanations of codebook redundancy, optimization instability, data/model scaling and SQ-Codec failure conditions. Appendices E-H discuss initialization confounds, decoder strength and sampling-error propagation. Rankings are qualified as high-level summaries, and uncontrolled tokenizer training differences are acknowledged. The earlier speech-only limitation is removed following the actual coverage expansion.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents TPE/Orion tuning over 20 trials, embedding initialization, ASR tokenization choices, TTS best-of-ten selection using Whisper Large, and sampling-search settings. Tokenizer metadata, checkpoint links, licenses and resource descriptions are expanded or revised. Access instructions shift toward a project website, but the public-availability claim conflicts with a footnote promising release with the camera-ready version.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded with ESPnet-Codec, VERSA, HEAR, newer tokenizers and broader speech, music and multimodal-model literature. The comparison with the already-cited Codec-SUPERB is rewritten around direct token evaluation versus waveform reconstruction, giving DASB a more explicit and stronger methodological novelty position.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and results narrative undergo extensive rewriting. v3 separates tokenizer selection from encoding, reorganizes results around domains, scaling, rankings and category trade-offs, and restructures the appendices around second-head results and additional analyses. Terminology also changes from 'compression' to 'acoustic' tokens.

P2.justification: Result tables are reorganized from bitrate blocks into tokenizer groups with codebook-count columns, and first-head results replace the main-text best-of-two summaries. Tokenizer metadata tables are redesigned, Figure 2 is redrawn, and new domain and ablation tables are added. Radar plots replace the earlier ranking table, while Figures 4-5 introduce TTS sensitivity plots.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves v1's acknowledged speech-only coverage limitation and materially strengthens assessment of benchmark stability through three-seed reporting, explicit tuning procedures and initialization/sampling analyses. These additions substantially improve usefulness and transparency. Undefined ± statistics, conflicting code-release statements and scaling arguments that mix datasets and languages remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical support and diagnostic depth are substantial overall.
